text: Metals bend far more easily than theory predicts because of dislocations: line defects that let atomic planes slip one row at a time. Three scientists proposed them independently in 1934.
In 1982 Dan Shechtman saw a crystal with tenfold diffraction symmetry, which periodic crystals cannot have. Linus Pauling, among others, rejected it; Shechtman won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
At everyday pressure, graphite is the more stable form of carbon, not diamond. Diamonds survive only because the conversion is so slow it effectively never happens.
Gallium is a solid metal on the shelf but melts at about 30 °C, so a gallium spoon melts away in a cup of hot tea, a classic laboratory prank.
Ruby and sapphire are the same mineral, corundum (aluminum oxide). A trace of chromium makes ruby red; traces of iron and titanium make sapphire blue.
In January 1943 the new tanker SS Schenectady split in two while moored at its dock in Portland, Oregon, in calm weather. Later research pointed to steel that turned brittle in the cold.
Dragline spider silk is about as strong as high-grade alloy steel at a sixth of the density. Silk from Darwin's bark spider is over 10 times tougher than Kevlar.
Snowflakes are six-sided because water molecules freeze into a hexagonal lattice. The six arms grow alike because each meets the same changing temperature and humidity as the flake falls.
Old church windows thicker at the bottom are not proof that glass flows. Medieval panes were simply uneven, and some were installed thick side up; at room temperature glass flow is immeasurably slow.
Geckos cling to ceilings using van der Waals forces: millions of microscopic hairs on their toes split into even finer nanoscale tips that touch the surface. No glue or suction is involved.
In 1998 the HIV drug ritonavir began crystallizing in a new, less soluble form that had never been seen before. Abbott had to withdraw the capsules, at a cost of over $250 million.
Tin-lead solder with 63 percent tin melts at 183 °C, below both pure tin (232 °C) and pure lead (327 °C). Such a lowest-melting mixture is called a eutectic.
Stretch most materials and they get thinner. Auxetic materials, such as specially structured foams, do the opposite: they grow fatter when pulled, a negative Poisson's ratio.
Quenching red-hot steel in water traps carbon atoms inside a strained iron crystal called martensite. That is why a blacksmith's quench makes a blade hard but brittle.
The Roman Lycurgus Cup, from the 4th century AD, looks jade green in reflected light and glows red when lit from within, thanks to gold and silver nanoparticles in its glass.
A quartz watch crystal is piezoelectric: voltage makes it flex, and flexing makes voltage. Its tuning fork is cut to vibrate 32,768 times a second, which is 2 to the 15th power.
Silly Putty came out of wartime research into synthetic rubber. It bounces when thrown, snaps when yanked, and slowly flows into a puddle if left alone.
Nitinol, a nickel-titanium alloy, can be crumpled and then spring back to its original shape when warmed. Its name stands for Nickel Titanium Naval Ordnance Laboratory.
Why liquids turn into glass, and whether a true phase transition lies hidden beneath the glass transition, remains an open problem in condensed matter physics.
Silica aerogel can be 99.8 percent empty space. NASA's Stardust probe used it to catch comet dust at about 6 km/s and bring it back to Earth in 2006.
In the 1950s Per-Ingvar Brånemark found that titanium chambers in rabbit bone had fused to the bone. This osseointegration led to the first modern dental implant in 1965.
In World War II Britain studied building an aircraft carrier from pykrete: ice mixed with about 14 percent sawdust, far tougher than plain ice and slower to melt (Project Habakkuk).
Ice VII, a form of ice that needs pressures of gigapascals, can stay solid well above 100 °C. In 2018 it was found trapped as inclusions inside natural diamonds from deep in the Earth.
In 1989 Don Eigler at IBM spelled out 'IBM' with 35 xenon atoms, using a scanning tunneling microscope to place individual atoms one by one.
Every periodic crystal belongs to one of just 14 lattice types (the Bravais lattices), and all their possible symmetries fall into exactly 230 space groups, worked out in the 1890s.
A topological insulator is an insulator inside but a conductor on its surface, and its topology protects those surface states. Bismuth selenide is a well-studied example.
Below 13.2 °C, shiny white tin can slowly crumble into gray powder, called tin pest. The story that it destroyed the buttons of Napoleon's army in Russia is probably a legend.
Whether Majorana zero modes, prized for building robust quantum computers, have truly been seen is disputed. A 2018 Nature paper claiming them in nanowires was retracted in 2021.
"What I want to talk about is the problem of manipulating and controlling things on a small scale." (Richard Feynman, "There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom", 1959)
John Goodenough shared the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the lithium-ion battery at age 97, making him the oldest Nobel laureate ever.
